newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Albright says Bosnia's presidents must pass budget.
newsitem.headline: Albright says Bosnia's presidents must pass budget.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Friday warned Bosnia's Moslem, Croat and Serb presidents that they will be denied $100 million in IMF loans and more than $1 billion in private donations until they pass a budget, her spokesman said.

Albright, leading a U.S. effort to increase international pressure on key parties to comply with the fraying Bosnia peace agreement, made her comments during a 15-minute meeting with the Balkan country's three chiefs -- Moslem Alija Izetbegovic, Croat Kresimir Zubak and Serb Momcilo Krajisnik.

Although senior U.S. officials this week have made similar threats to Bosnia's leaders, this is the first time that Albright made the point to them directly. She will visit the Balkans this weekend to carry further her campaign for compliance with the 1995 U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accord.
"The price of the $100 million is to pass a budget law," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
Albright "specifically asked them to work hard on a new law that needs to be agreed to further the Bosnian state", he said.
He stressed that this was not a unilateral U.S. threat but a common International Monetary Fund practice to condition its assistance on reforms. The United States has an effective veto at the IMF.
Albright told the presidents that an international conference on Bosnia, which is expected to raise an estimated $1.4 billion, could not go forward until the budget was enacted, Burns said.
Under the Dayton peace accord, Bosnia is supposed to be a unified state with two separate entities, one for Serbs and the other a Croat-Moslem federation.
But Bosnia's ethnic factions have resisted integration and some U.S. officials believe they are not truly interested in peace.

Agreeing on a common budget is one essential tool of a unified state. The three presidents finally reached agreement this week on a law establishing a central bank and they have also finally agreed on a customs law, accomplishments Albright praised, Burns said.

With 30,000 NATO-led stabilisation force (SFOR) troops in Bosnia that are due to leave next June, Washington and its allies are increasingly concerned that their time for ensuring that fighting does not re-ignite next year is running out.
The major western powers involved in Bosnia -- the United States, Britain, Germany, France and Russia -- were to meet with the Bosnian parties in Sintra later on Friday following a NATO meeting.

Burns said all three presidents "pledged to work together" to get the budget agreed. After Albright left the meeting, the Bosnian officials met with senior members of Albright's team, including new U.S. envoy Robert Gelbard, and Carl Bildt, the international envoy for Bosnia, to continue work on the budget and other issues.
The spokesman described Krajisnik as having told Albright one half of the Bosnian Serb republic was eager for her to visit Bosnia and the other half "fears you".

Albright was also to meet in Sintra with Biljana Plavsic, the president of the Serb republic. The United States has tried to work with Plavsic as part of the peace process but Bosnian Serb hardliners have sought to prevent her cooperation.
